summary: Defines extensions to XMPP core that provide basic instant messaging and presence, meeting requirements set out in RFC 2779. It is a proposed standard and obsoletes RFC 3921.

eli5.summary: Built on the XMPP chat language, this adds the features people expect from a chat app: sending messages and showing whether friends are online.

questions: what is xmpp instant messaging and presence
how do xmpp presence subscriptions work
subtitle: How XMPP turns a stream of XML into a chat app: contact lists, who-is-online presence, and one-to-one messages.

tldr.problem: XMPP core only moves XML stanzas between parties. An instant messaging service also needs a contact list, a way to share who is online with approved people only, and conventions for chat messages.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6121 defines a roster managed with IQ stanzas, presence stanzas that carry both availability and subscription requests, message stanzas with a small set of types, and the rules servers follow to deliver all of them.
tldr.outcome: It meets the requirements of RFC 2779 for basic instant messaging and presence, obsoletes RFC 3921, and drops the old session-establishment step.

today: RFC 6121 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 3921. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, so it is the definition of XMPP instant messaging and presence in this collection.

sections.title: What XMPP IM Adds to XMPP
sections.content:
The Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP) is an application profile of XML for the near-real-time exchange of structured data. Its core features provide building blocks. RFC 6121 defines the extensions on top that give the basic functionality expected of an instant messaging (IM) and presence application, as described in RFC 2779.

The RFC names four traditional ingredients of IM: a list of contacts (the roster), short text messages exchanged in a one-to-one chat session, presence (who is available), and presence given only to contacts the user has authorized through a presence subscription. From these it derives four use cases: manage contacts, exchange messages, exchange presence, and manage presence subscriptions.

A typical session, after the XML stream is negotiated, is: retrieve the roster, send initial presence to go online, exchange messages and manage subscriptions and roster entries, then send unavailable presence and close the stream. The older RFC 3921 had one more step, formal session establishment. Experience showed it was unnecessary, though an implementation MAY still offer it for backward compatibility.
sections.eli5: XMPP is like a phone line that can carry any note. This RFC adds the chat-app parts on top: a contacts list, a green light for who is online, and ways to send messages.

sections.title: The Roster
sections.content:
A user's roster is their contact list. It is stored by the user's server on the user's behalf, so the user can see it from any device. The server SHOULD store roster data unmodified if possible, MUST return it to an authorized client, and MUST restrict access so that only authorized entities (typically the account owner) can read or change it.

Rosters are managed with <iq/> stanzas carrying a <query/> element in the jabber:iq:roster namespace. Each contact is an <item/> with a required jid, an optional name handle chosen by the user, and any number of <group/> children, so groups are not exclusive. A client asks for the roster with a roster get, the server answers with a roster result, a client changes it with a roster set containing exactly one item, and the server tells every interested resource about changes with a roster push.

The subscription attribute records the presence relationship: none (the default), to, from or both. In a roster set the value remove deletes the item. The server-set ask and approved attributes report pending outbound requests and pre-approvals, and a client MUST NOT send them.

Roster versioning saves bandwidth. The server stamps the roster with an opaque ver string. A reconnecting client can send the last version it saw, and the server either returns the full roster or an empty result followed by roster pushes for only the items that changed.
sections.eli5: The roster is your address book, kept safely at the chat company so every phone and laptop of yours shows the same list. Each entry also remembers whether you can see each other's online light.

sections.title: Presence Subscriptions
sections.content:
To protect privacy, presence is disclosed only to entities the user has approved. Such an approved entity has a subscription to the user's presence. A subscription lasts across presence sessions, until the contact unsubscribes or the user cancels it. The RFC notes this differs from the model used for presence subscriptions in SIP.

Subscriptions are managed with presence stanzas of four types. A subscribe asks for permission to see a contact's presence, and it is addressed to the contact's bare JID, not a full JID. The contact answers with subscribed to approve. Later, unsubscribe ends a subscription the sender holds and unsubscribed denies a request or cancels one already granted. The server stamps these with the sender's bare JID, which helps prevent presence leaks.

A contact's server MUST NOT automatically approve a subscription request on the contact's behalf. A user can also pre-approve a request by sending subscribed before any request arrives.

Appendix A describes the user's side as four primary states (None, To, From, Both), refined by pending-in and pending-out sub-states into nine possible subscription states.
sections.eli5: Before you can see a friend's online light you must ask, and they must say yes. Once they agree it stays that way until one of you changes your mind.

sections.title: Exchanging Presence
sections.content:
Presence is availability for communication. A presence stanza with no type means available, and one with type of unavailable means not. There is no available value. Presence follows a publish-subscribe pattern: the client sends presence to its server with no to address, and the server broadcasts it to every contact with a subscription.

A client goes online by sending initial presence, ideally after requesting the roster. The server sends it from the user's full JID to every contact whose roster state is from or both, and also to the user's own other available resources. Because the server may lack presence about the user's contacts, it also sends presence probes, which are presence stanzas of type probe that request a contact's current presence. Clients SHOULD NOT send probes. A client can also send directed presence, with a to address, to someone who is not subscribed.

Presence can carry three optional children. <show/> is one of away, chat, dnd or xa, and its absence means plain available. <status/> is human-readable text, repeated only with distinct xml:lang values. <priority/> is an integer from -128 to +127, treated as zero when missing, and the server MAY override it.
sections.eli5: Going online is like turning on a porch light that only your approved friends can see. You can also add a little note, like "busy", next to the light.

sections.title: Messages and Chat Sessions
sections.content:
A message stanza pushes information to another entity. Its type attribute is RECOMMENDED and must be one of chat, error, groupchat, headline or normal. Normal is the default, and an application that sees no type, or one it does not understand, MUST treat the message as normal.

The usual children are <body/> (human-readable text, repeated only with distinct xml:lang values), <subject/> and <thread/>. Messages may also carry extended content from other namespaces.

For a one-to-one chat session, the client SHOULD use type chat and include a <thread/> in the first message, and the contact's client SHOULD preserve both in replies. The first message goes to the contact's bare JID. After a reply arrives from a full JID, the client SHOULD address further messages to that full JID, which the RFC calls locking in. It unlocks and returns to the bare JID when it hears from another resource of the same peer.

If two parties chat without a presence subscription, they SHOULD send each other directed presence so each can tell if the other goes offline. A client MUST let the user disable this globally or per entity.
sections.eli5: When you start chatting, you first call out to a person's name. Once one of their devices answers, you talk to that exact device until another one speaks up.

sections.title: Server Delivery Rules
sections.content:
Section 8 tells servers what to do with a stanza depending on its address and on the state of the target account. A stanza with no to address is handled by the server for the sending account. A stanza for a remote domain is routed to that domain. For a local user, the server checks whether the account exists, whether it has available resources, and whether the to address is a bare JID or a full JID that matches a resource.

Two concerns shape the rules: directory harvesting attacks, where someone probes to learn which accounts exist, and presence leaks. Where a rule offers a choice of silently ignoring a stanza or returning an error, the server SHOULD return an error when the sender is in the user's roster, is authorized to receive the user's presence, or has received directed presence from the user, since in those cases an error reveals nothing new.

Message delivery to a bare JID depends on presence priority. Resources with negative priority do not receive bare-JID messages. With several non-negative resources, a normal message goes to the "most available" resource or resources by the server's own algorithm, and a headline message goes to all of them. Chat messages should reach all resources only if clients can explicitly opt in. An offline account may have the message stored for later or bounced, according to the rules summarized in a table in the RFC.
sections.eli5: The chat company acts like a mail room. It looks at the address on each note, checks whether the person is in, and then decides whether to hand it over, hold it, or send it back.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
RFC 6121 relies on the core XMPP security discussion for channel encryption, authentication, information leaks, denial of service and federation. A user places trust in their server, so the server should preferably require channel encryption, authenticate any client that accesses the account, and correctly process the user's stanzas, rosters, subscriptions, probes and presence broadcasts.

Even then, the client has no assurance that stanzas are protected on every hop or inside a server. A client that wants end-to-end confidentiality and integrity must apply its own encryption and signing of XML stanzas.

The IM-specific rules are mostly about presence. A server MUST NOT reveal a user's presence in answer to a probe from an entity that is not authorized, and MUST NOT leak availability to unauthorized entities generally. A client MAY ignore the <status/> text in subscription stanzas, which can help prevent presence subscription spam.
sections.eli5: Your chat company is trusted to keep your online light private, so it only shows it to people you approved. If you want your messages locked so even the company cannot read them, you have to lock them yourself.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 3921
sections.content:
RFC 6121 reflects deployment and interoperability-testing experience since RFC 3921 was published in October 2004. Appendix E lists the substantive changes. The session-establishment protocol was removed, although servers are encouraged to keep advertising it as a no-op. Roster versioning and optional pre-approved subscriptions with the approved attribute were added. Probes now come from the bare JID, the default priority of zero was stated, and an optional parent attribute was added to <thread/>.

Error handling for subscriptions, probes and notifications was clarified so that out-of-sync rosters on different servers repair more smoothly. Servers may use their own algorithm to pick the most available resource. Communications blocking went back to XEP-0016, and the recommendation to support the _im and _pres SRV records was removed.
sections.eli5: This is the second edition of the rulebook. The authors dropped a step nobody needed and added shortcuts that save time, based on what they learned from real chat programs.

viz.caption: SIMPLIFIED SUBSCRIPTION REQUEST AND APPROVAL (SUMMARY, NOT A TRANSCRIPT)

messages.label: presence type=subscribe
messages.note: Addressed to the contact's bare JID.

messages.label: subscribe
messages.note: The server MUST NOT approve on the contact's behalf.

items.label: available
items.desc: No type attribute means the entity is available.

items.label: Unavailable
items.desc: The sender is no longer available.

items.label: Subscribe
items.desc: The sender wishes to subscribe to the recipient's presence.

items.label: Subscribed
items.desc: The sender has allowed the recipient to receive their presence.

items.label: Unsubscribe
items.desc: The sender is unsubscribing from the receiver's presence.

items.label: Unsubscribed
items.desc: A request was denied or a granted subscription was canceled.

items.label: Probe
items.desc: A request for current presence, generated only by a server.

items.label: Error
items.desc: An error occurred processing a presence stanza; must include an error element.

items.label: Normal
items.desc: A standalone message to which a reply is expected. The default.

items.label: Chat
items.desc: Sent in a one-to-one chat session.

items.label: Groupchat
items.desc: Sent in a multi-user chat environment.

items.label: Headline
items.desc: An alert or notification to which no reply is expected.

items.label: Error
items.desc: Generated by an entity that hit an error processing a message.
